people.name: Bryan Thao Worra
body: In 2012, when the world gathered in London for the Summer Olympics, a poet from the Twin Cities was there representing Laos, not as an athlete but as a Cultural Olympian at the Southbank Centre. For Bryan Thao Worra, it was one more step in a long effort to put Lao voices on the world stage.

He was born in Vientiane, Laos, in 1973 and was adopted that year by a pilot flying in Laos, who brought him to the United States. Poets & Writers says he was raised in Saline, Michigan. He later connected with Lao community life as an adult in Minnesota, where thousands of Lao refugees had resettled after 1975.

His writing blends Lao history, the legacy of war, refugee memory, and a love of science fiction, horror and fantasy. His books include On the Other Side of the Eye (2007), Winter Ink (2008), Barrow (2009) and Demonstra (2013). In 2009 he received a National Endowment for the Arts Fellowship in Literature for poetry, which AGNI and Purdue University describe as a first for a Lao American. He has edited Bakka Magazine, a Laotian literary arts journal, and Purdue says he has served as the Lao Minnesotan Poet Laureate since 2018.

He has been just as devoted to building community as to writing. He co-founded Sahtu Press in 2013 and received a Joyce Award in 2019. In April 2025, MPR News described him as chair of the community board of the state's Council on Asian Pacific Minnesotans and as the leader of a project with the Lao Assistance Center of Minnesota that uses poetry and creative writing to record 50 years of Lao refugee stories. MPR credits the 2024 exhibit Laomerica 50: Democracy and Diaspora at Minneapolis Central Library to the SEALit Center, the literary organization behind that project. He was poet in residence at Purdue in fall 2025.
keyFacts: 1973: Born in Vientiane, Laos.
2007 to 2013: Published On the Other Side of the Eye, Winter Ink, Barrow and Demonstra.
2009: National Endowment for the Arts Fellowship in poetry.
2012: Cultural Olympian representing Laos at the London Games.
2013: Co-founded Sahtu Press.
Since 2018: Lao Minnesotan Poet Laureate.
2019: Joyce Award.
Fall 2025: Poet in residence, Purdue University.
people.connectToWork: When your intake form or conversation assumes how someone came to belong to a community, what happens to a person who grew up apart from it, such as an adoptee?

people.name: Saymoukda Duangphouxay Vongsay
body: In Kung Fu Zombies Vs Cannibals and Kung Fu Zombies Vs Shaman Warrior, Saymoukda Duangphouxay Vongsay used action and humor to tell stories of war and displacement on Twin Cities stages.

Vongsay was born in a refugee camp in Nong Khai, Thailand, just across the Mekong River from Laos. Her family resettled in Minnesota in the mid-1980s, and she is based in Saint Paul. She earned a BA in English from the University of Minnesota, Morris, in 2005 and a Master of Liberal Studies from the University of Minnesota in 2017.

Her writing moves across forms. Her book When Everything Was Everything reflects on childhood in a refugee family, and she has been developing a musical, In the Camps: A Refugee Musical. In 2020 she and Theater Mu, the Twin Cities' Asian American theater company, received an Andrew W. Mellon Foundation grant through the National Playwright Residency Program, making her a full-time playwright in residence at Mu for three years. She was named a 2022 Bush Fellow.

Mid-1980s: Family resettled in Minnesota.
2005: BA in English, University of Minnesota, Morris.
2017: Master of Liberal Studies, University of Minnesota.
2020: Mellon Foundation National Playwright Residency at Theater Mu.

people.name: Ann Ahmed
body: In 2023 The New York Times included Gai Noi, a Lao restaurant in Minneapolis's Loring Park area, on its list of 50 favorite restaurants in the country. Chef Ann Ahmed had opened it that May, and the list brought national attention to Lao food served under its own name.
Ahmed was born in Laos and came to Minnesota with her family at age 4, sponsored to come to the United States more than four decades ago.

She built her career step by step. In 2005 she opened Lemon Grass Thai in Brooklyn Park, which ran for about 18 years. In 2018 she opened Lat14 Asian Eatery in Golden Valley, named for the 14th parallel north, the latitude line that touches Laos, Vietnam, Cambodia, the Philippines and Thailand. In fall 2021 came Khâluna in south Minneapolis.

The James Beard Foundation named her a semifinalist for Best Chef: Midwest in 2023 and for Outstanding Chef in 2025. Mpls.St.Paul Magazine included Gai Noi in its 2026 list of the 50 best restaurants in the Twin Cities.

2023 and 2025: James Beard Award semifinalist.

people.name: Sunny Chanthanouvong
body: In North Minneapolis stands one of the North Side's oldest organizations, the Lao Assistance Center of Minnesota, founded in 1983 to help newly arrived refugee families with the basics of a new life. Since 2003 it has been led by Sunny Chanthanouvong, who came to the United States as a Lao refugee with his own family.

His path into community leadership began in the 1990s. While studying computer science in college, he started working with Lao young people. In 2003 he became the center's executive director, and as of October 2026 the center's website still lists him in that role.

By the American Immigration Council's 2022 account, he encourages families to keep their traditions while pursuing education, small business ownership, and better access to health care and housing. He helped bring the Lao National Conference and the first Lao American Writers Summit to Minneapolis, and he helped develop Legacies of War: Refugee Nation Twin Cities, an exhibit about the unexploded bombs that still contaminate Laos.
His service has been recognized with the Virginia McKnight Binger Unsung Hero Award and a Bush Leadership Fellowship.
keyFacts: 1990s: Began working with Lao youth while studying computer science.
2003: Became executive director of the Lao Assistance Center of Minnesota.
Helped bring the Lao National Conference and first Lao American Writers Summit to Minneapolis.
Honors: Virginia McKnight Binger Unsung Hero Award; Bush Leadership Fellowship.
people.connectToWork: Before you plan outreach, which long-standing local organizations have already done this work, and how would you approach them as partners, including paying for their time?

people.name: Chanida Phaengdara Potter
body: In January 2015, at the Vine Arts Center in Minneapolis, a Lao American writer opened an exhibit called Refuge of the InvisibLao. For two years she had asked Lao people around the world for photographs. Chanida Phaengdara Potter told MPR News the work was deeply personal.

Sahtu Press reported in 2017 that she was born in a re-education camp at Vieng Xai, Laos. MPR News says she learned to walk in a Thai refugee camp and grew up in North Minneapolis in a home where her parents spoke only Lao to her. She earned a bachelor's degree in global studies and media studies from the University of Minnesota–Twin Cities and a master of public administration from Hamline University.

She served as chief editor of Little Laos on the Prairie, which gave Lao Americans a place to write about their own lives, and was founding executive director of The SEAD Project for about a decade. The project, founded in 2011 by the University of Minnesota's account, works with Hmong, Khmer, Lao and Vietnamese Minnesotans, who share a history of war and refugee resettlement but have distinct languages and cultures. She co-authored Planting SEADS, described as Minnesota's first collection of Hmong, Khmer, Lao and Viet Minnesotan stories, poetry and art.
As of May 2026 the University of Minnesota names other people as The SEAD Project's co-executive directors, so her leadership there is part of its history.
keyFacts: Chief editor, Little Laos on the Prairie.
2015: Organized the Refuge of the InvisibLao exhibit in Minneapolis.
Founding executive director of The SEAD Project for about a decade.
Co-authored Planting SEADS.
people.connectToWork: If a report or form groups people as "Southeast Asian", what differences in language and history does that hide, and how would you get data that keeps them apart?

people.name: Kulap Vilaysack
body: In 1993, Kulap Vilaysack's mother accidentally revealed something she had never meant to say: the man Kulap had always called Dad was not her biological father. Kulap was 14. Years later she turned that moment into Origin Story, a documentary following her search for her biological father in Laos.

Vilaysack was born in Washington, D.C., to Lao parents who had fled Laos and lived in a refugee camp in Thailand. The family moved to Minnesota and settled in Eagan. After high school she moved to Los Angeles and studied comedy at the Upright Citizens Brigade Theatre.

She built a career across comedy and media. She hosted the Earwolf comedy podcast Who Charted? beginning in late 2010, and she created Bajillion Dollar Propertie$, a parody of real estate reality shows, for the streaming service Seeso.
Origin Story was released in 2019, including on Amazon Prime. It looks at refugee marriages and the relationship between Lao parents and their American-raised children.
keyFacts: Born in Washington, D.C.; raised in Eagan, Minnesota.
1993: Learned at 14 that her father was not her biological father.
2010: Began hosting the Who Charted? podcast.
Created Bajillion Dollar Propertie$ for Seeso.
2019: Origin Story released.
people.connectToWork: When you ask about family history on a form or in a meeting, what could you do so a person can choose what to share and when?

people.name: Thavisouk Phrasavath
body: In early 2009, a film made over 23 years was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature. The Betrayal (Nerakhoon) tells of a Lao family's journey from war-torn Laos to New York and their struggle to survive in Brooklyn. Its co-director and editor, Thavisouk Phrasavath, was also its subject.

After the communist government took power in 1975, people connected to the old government and to the Americans faced imprisonment and re-education camps. By the film's POV description, Phrasavath's father, an officer in the Royal Lao Army, had joined a secret CIA-organized force, collected intelligence and helped guide U.S. B-52 bombing runs. He was declared an enemy of the state and taken away. By POV's account, the family did not know whether he had been sent to a labor camp or executed. The family made its way to the United States and rebuilt its life in Brooklyn.

He met cinematographer Ellen Kuras when she sought him out to learn the Lao language; the International Documentary Association says he was then a 19-year-old community leader in Brooklyn. Their twice-weekly lessons became an exchange of stories about Lao beliefs, philosophy and his family's history, and over time he became the documentary's subject and then her co-director. Voice of America's Lao service called it the first documentary directed by a Lao American.

The film was a co-production with American Documentary | POV, funded in part by the Center for Asian American Media. Its Oscar nomination brought the secret war in Laos and Lao refugee life to a wide audience.
keyFacts: After 1975: Family left Laos and resettled in Brooklyn.
Taught Lao to Ellen Kuras, which led to the film.
2008: The Betrayal (Nerakhoon) released after 23 years in the making.
2009: Nominated for the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature.
people.connectToWork: If a person is cautious about giving information to a government office, how would you explain what is shared and with whom, without assuming why they are cautious?

people.name: Seng Luangrath
body: In the late 2000s, at a Thai restaurant in northern Virginia, customers began hearing about dishes that were not on the menu: Lao specialties such as papaya salad and laab. The cook behind them, Seng Luangrath, was testing whether diners were ready for the food of her homeland. They were.

Luangrath, from Vientiane, fled Laos in 1981 at age 12 with her mother, uncle and two brothers after her father was taken to a labor camp. They crossed the Mekong by boat into Thailand, and in refugee camps there she learned to cook dishes from across Laos. Arlington Magazine says she spent two years in a camp, settled with her family in Berkeley, California, and moved to Virginia in 1989. She took over Bangkok Golden in Falls Church with no prior restaurant experience and slowly introduced Lao cooking. In 2017 it was renamed Padaek, after the fermented fish sauce used in Lao cooking.

In 2014 she opened Thip Khao on 14th Street NW in Washington's Columbia Heights neighborhood, with her son, chef Bobby Pradachith, as co-owner. It was widely reported as the city's first Lao restaurant. As of October 2026 the Michelin Guide lists Thip Khao and names her as chef and co-owner. The James Beard Foundation named her a semifinalist for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic in 2018, her second such nomination in two years.

She leads the Lao Food Movement, which promotes Lao cuisine and culture and encourages young Lao cooks to open Lao restaurants rather than present their food as Thai. PBS NewsHour and the Smithsonian's Center for Folklife and Cultural Heritage have featured her work.
keyFacts: 1981: Fled Laos at age 12; lived in Thai refugee camps.
Took over Bangkok Golden in Falls Church, Virginia (renamed Padaek in 2017).
2014: Opened Thip Khao in Columbia Heights, Washington, D.C.
Leads the Lao Food Movement.
James Beard semifinalist, Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic.

people.name: Ova Saopeng
body: After a trip to Laos to visit relatives, actor Ova Saopeng and his wife and creative partner, Leilani Chan, came home troubled by the poverty and lingering war damage they had seen and by stories that were rarely told aloud. The result was Refugee Nation, a play about three generations of Lao refugees in America.
Saopeng is a refugee from Laos who has made it his work to bring refugee and immigrant experiences to the American stage.

Refugee Nation, created with Chan through their Los Angeles company TeAda Productions, was built from interviews with Lao immigrants, many in the Twin Cities. MPR News reported that themes kept recurring: disconnection between generations, young men drawn to gangs, and a lost sense of identity. The play toured communities across the country, including Minneapolis, where it ran at Intermedia Arts in 2010, co-presented by the Lao Assistance Center and Pangea World Theater. The University of California, Irvine's Southeast Asian Archive holds recordings and promotional materials from the production.

As of October 2026 TeAda lists him as associate artistic director. He works as an actor, playwright and teaching artist, and his credits include Masters of the Currents, Global Taxi Driver and Native Immigrant.
keyFacts: Refugee from Laos; actor, playwright and teaching artist.
Co-created Refugee Nation with Leilani Chan through TeAda Productions.
2010: Refugee Nation performed at Intermedia Arts, Minneapolis.
Associate artistic director, TeAda Productions.

people.name: Nor Sanavongsay
body: In December 2013, Nor Sanavongsay released a children's book called A Sticky Mess, starring Xieng Mieng, a clever trickster from Lao folktales. To publish it after a Kickstarter campaign, he co-founded his own press, Sahtu Press.

By Sahtu Press's account, he arrived in the United States as a Lao refugee at age three, on January 29, 1979, first settling with his family in Tennessee. In 2020 the press described him as a UX designer at Workday living in the San Francisco Bay Area. He founded the press alongside Bryan Thao Worra and Krysada Binly Phounsiri as a Lao American-owned literary publisher. He wrote and illustrated A Sticky Mess and illustrated Mommy Eats Fried Grasshoppers.

Sahtu Press marked its tenth anniversary in 2023. In 2020 several of his artworks, including the digital piece Sabaidee Laos, were accepted into the collection of the Barack Obama Presidential Center. He has been a member of the Lao Artists Festival of Elgin, Illinois. Most of what is published about him comes from the press he co-founded.
keyFacts: January 29, 1979: Arrived in the U.S. (Tennessee) as a refugee, age three.
2013: Co-founded Sahtu Press and published A Sticky Mess.
Illustrated Mommy Eats Fried Grasshoppers.
2020: Artworks accepted into the Obama Presidential Center collection.
2023: Sahtu Press marked 10 years.

people.name: Channapha Khamvongsa
body: In September 2016, Barack Obama became the first sitting U.S. president to visit Laos. While there, he publicly acknowledged the work of a Lao American woman who had spent more than a decade pressing Washington to face what it had left behind: millions of unexploded bombs. That woman was Channapha Khamvongsa.

She was born in Vientiane in 1973. In 1979, when she was six, her family fled Laos and spent a year in a refugee camp on the Thai border before being accepted for resettlement in the United States. She grew up in Virginia, earned a bachelor's degree in public administration from George Mason University in 2000 and a master's in public policy from Georgetown University in 2002.

Americans Who Tell the Truth reports that the United States dropped an estimated 260 to 270 million cluster submunitions on Laos during the Vietnam War era, and that about 80 million did not explode. Those bombs still kill and injure people in Laos today.

In 2004 Khamvongsa founded Legacies of War to educate Americans about the bombing and to push for cleanup and help for victims. Under her leadership, annual U.S. funding for bomb clearance and victim assistance in Laos rose from an average of about $2 million in 2008 to $30 million in 2016. She led the organization until 2019. She had earlier worked at the Ford Foundation and NEO Philanthropy, and Georgetown's public policy school gave her its Distinguished Alumni Award. Her Legacies of War biography lists her as managing director and chief strategist at Vong Law Group.
keyFacts: 1973: Born in Vientiane, Laos.
1979: Family fled Laos; a year in a Thai border refugee camp, then resettlement in the U.S.
2000 and 2002: Degrees from George Mason University and Georgetown University.
2004: Founded Legacies of War.
2016: Recognized by President Obama during his visit to Laos.
2019: Stepped down from leading Legacies of War.
people.connectToWork: How could you learn about a history like this before you meet someone, so that the person you serve does not have to teach it to you?

people.name: Catzie Vilayphonh
body: In 2000, a Lao American poet and two other young Asian American women who had just met at a writers' workshop in Philadelphia entered a local round of a touring Def Poetry Slam. Calling themselves Yellow Rage, they made the semifinals. Within days Def Jam flew them to New York to audition for a new show being pitched to HBO. Catzie Vilayphonh and her partner Michelle Myers went on to appear on Russell Simmons Presents Def Poetry. The Leeway Foundation calls her one of the first Asian American women on the show.

Vilayphonh was born in a refugee camp and has said she has never been to Laos, the country her family comes from. Yellow Rage became known for poems confronting stereotypes of Asian American women, and the group became a duo after the third founding member left for medical school.

She has lived and worked in South Philadelphia. Through her project Laos in the House, she promotes storytelling among Lao American refugees through art. In 2015 she curated a gallery exhibit of Lao artists, and the project grew into a video series; she taught herself photography and filmmaking to make it. In August 2010 she led the organization of the first Lao American Writers Summit, in Minneapolis. The summit later met in San Diego and near Seattle. She has also served on the board of 1Love Movement, which fights the deportation of Southeast Asian refugees, and on Philadelphia's Mayor's Commission on Asian American Affairs.
keyFacts: Born in a refugee camp.
2000: Co-founded Yellow Rage in Philadelphia.
Early 2000s: Performed on HBO's Russell Simmons Presents Def Poetry.
August 2010: Led organization of the first Lao American Writers Summit, Minneapolis.
2015: Curated an exhibit of Lao artists through Laos in the House.
Board member, 1Love Movement; appointee, Philadelphia Mayor's Commission on Asian American Affairs.
people.connectToWork: When a record says someone is "from" a country, what are you assuming about what they remember or know of it? How would you ask instead?

people.name: Xay Khamsyvoravong
body: On December 1, 2022, the city council of Newport, Rhode Island, chose as its mayor the man who had just been the top vote-getter in the city's at-large council race. Xay Khamsyvoravong, the son of a refugee from Laos, called Newport his hometown.

He graduated from Brown University and Roger Williams University School of Law. He was deputy chief of staff to Rhode Island's general treasurer from 2007 to 2010, managed Frank Caprio's 2010 campaign for governor, chaired Providence Water from 2013 to 2021, and spent about 15 years in business, including as a senior vice president at Webster Bank.

As mayor, he drew talk of higher office. In February 2023, when a U.S. House seat opened, he said he would stay in Newport. He was re-elected to the council at large in 2024, while another councilor became mayor. In March 2026 he entered the Democratic primary for lieutenant governor of Rhode Island, and in the September 9, 2026, primary the Associated Press projected incumbent Sabina Matos the winner over him and three others. As of October 2026 the City of Newport lists him as a councilor at large.

people.name: Justin Phongsavanh
body: On June 19, 2021, at Breck High School in Minneapolis, a wheelchair javelin thrower from Iowa launched a throw of 33.29 meters at the U.S. Paralympic Team Trials, a world record. Weeks later, Justin Phongsavanh won bronze at the Tokyo Paralympics.
Phongsavanh was born in Des Moines, Iowa, to one Lao and one white parent. After time in Iowa's foster care system, he was adopted by Tamera Shinn and raised in Ankeny, outside Des Moines.

In October 2015, at age 18, he was shot in the parking lot of an Ankeny McDonald's. The bullet punctured his lung and a fragment lodged in his spine, leaving him paralyzed. He turned to adaptive sports and found javelin. He won gold at the 2017 U.S. Paralympics Track and Field Nationals and gold at the 2019 Parapan American Games in Lima, Peru, before his record-setting throw in Minneapolis and his Tokyo medal. He competed at the 2023 Parapan American Games in Santiago, Chile, and placed fourth at the Paris 2024 Paralympics.

October 2015: Paralyzed after being shot in Ankeny, at age 18.
2017: Gold, U.S. Paralympics Track and Field Nationals.
2019: Gold, javelin, Parapan American Games, Lima.
June 19, 2021: World record of 33.29 m at U.S. Paralympic Trials, Minneapolis.
2021: Bronze, Tokyo Paralympics.
2024: Fourth, javelin, Paris Paralympics.
people.connectToWork: If a person's disability and heritage both matter to them, does your process let them speak to both, or does it send them to two different doors?

people.name: Bob Malaythong
body: In August 2008, at the Beijing Olympics, a badminton player born in Vientiane, Laos, took the court for the United States in men's doubles. Khan "Bob" Malaythong and his partner Howard Bach won their opening match before losing to a Chinese pair, and tied for fifth. Speaking to Voice of America's Lao service, he said he was very proud to be the first Lao American athlete to have come that far.

Malaythong was born in Vientiane on April 10, 1981, and moved to the United States at age eight; his brother-in-law had him practicing badminton four days a week. He graduated from Palmer High School in Colorado Springs in 2000 and earned an associate degree from Santa Ana College in California in 2006. Team USA lists his hometown as Rockville, Maryland.

Team USA credits him with U.S. national men's doubles titles in 2003 and 2005, the 2005 mixed doubles title, and U.S. Adult National men's doubles titles in 2006 and 2007. At the 2007 Pan American Games in Rio de Janeiro he won silver in men's doubles with Bach and, by Olympedia's record, bronze in mixed doubles.
keyFacts: 1981: Born in Vientiane, Laos; moved to the U.S. at age 8.
2000: Graduated from Palmer High School, Colorado Springs.
2006: Associate degree, Santa Ana College.
2003 to 2007: Several U.S. national doubles titles.
2007: Pan American Games silver (men's doubles) and bronze (mixed doubles).
2008: Tied for fifth in men's doubles at the Beijing Olympics.

institutions.name: Lao Assistance Center of Minnesota
body: The Lao Assistance Center of Minnesota was founded in 1983 by ethnic Lao to support refugees arriving in the state. The American Immigration Council calls it one of the oldest organizations in North Minneapolis. Sunny Chanthanouvong, profiled on this page, has led it since 2003.

Its website describes culturally relevant food assistance, help finding a way through systems, and advocacy on housing, employment, education and public benefits, for low-income, limited-English speaking people, families and elders. Its history names past work including English classes, citizenship preparation, youth academic support, a Lao culture camp, and in-language mental health outreach. GiveMN says it has run five programs serving more than 750 low- to moderate-income Lao families a year. The center's own About page says it serves "over 5,000 low-income, limited-English speaking individuals, families, and elders." The two figures count different things (families a year versus individuals) and date from different times.

In 2010 it co-presented Refugee Nation in Minneapolis, and it helped develop the Legacies of War exhibit in the Twin Cities. In April 2025 MPR News reported that it was working with the SEALit Center, under a Minnesota Historical Society grant, on a project recording 50 years of Lao refugee stories.
No source was found showing that the center provides disability-specific services, so call and ask before referring anyone for them. The center's main line is (612) 374-4967.
keyFacts: 1983: Founded by ethnic Lao to support refugees.
2003: Sunny Chanthanouvong became executive director.
2010: Co-presented Refugee Nation at Intermedia Arts.
2025: Partner in a Minnesota Historical Society grant project on Lao refugee stories.
institutions.connectToWork: If you ask a community organization to help reach families, what will your agency do in return, and how will you avoid sending it work your own staff should do?

institutions.name: Legacies of War
body: Legacies of War began with drawings. Founder Channapha Khamvongsa built early public programs around a set of original drawings of the bombing, a collection the organization still says "started it all". From that start in 2004 it became a national voice on the bombing of Laos and its aftermath.

Its mission is to raise awareness of the U.S. bombings during the American wars in Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam, provide space for healing, and push for clearing unexploded ordnance. Through education and lobbying, it helped increase U.S. funding for bomb clearance and victim assistance in Laos from about $2 million a year in 2008 to $30 million in 2016. In Minnesota, its traveling exhibit was part of Legacies of War: Refugee Nation Twin Cities, developed with the Lao Assistance Center of Minnesota.

The organization describes itself as Lao American and women-led. As of October 2026 its website reports at least 21 injuries and one death from explosive ordnance so far in 2026, across seven provinces of Laos, and says only about 10 percent of the unexploded ordnance in Laos has been cleared. It counts these itself. Its About page names Sera Koulabdara as CEO and says it is a project of the FCNL Education Fund.
keyFacts: 2004: Founded by Channapha Khamvongsa.
2008 to 2016: U.S. clearance funding for Laos rose from about $2 million to $30 million a year.
2016: Recognized by President Obama in Laos.
Project of the FCNL Education Fund, Washington, D.C.
institutions.connectToWork: For someone whose relatives still live with this danger, what would you want to know before asking about family in Laos, and how would you let them decide whether to discuss it?

institutions.name: Lao Temple Siri Buddharam
institutions.location: Rural Nobles County, just outside Worthington
body: For Lao families in southwestern Minnesota, the nearest temple once meant a long drive to the Twin Cities, and getting a monk for a ceremony was hard. So local Lao residents set out to build their own. Nobles County changed its ordinances to allow a church in an agricultural area, and after a long permitting process the temple was officially established in 2004 on a rural site near Worthington. The local paper calls it the city's first Buddhist temple. The paper spelled the name Siri in 2015 and Sri in 2022.

In April 2015 the Worthington newspaper reported that two monks lived at the temple and that about 150 people attended monthly services, coming from Worthington, Jackson, Mountain Lake and Magnolia, and from Sioux Falls, South Dakota, and Sibley, Iowa. Four large celebrations a year drew hundreds of people. Temple president Saksady "Scotty" Xaisongkham worked at the local JBS plant and was a vice president of United Food and Commercial Workers Local 1161, and the paper reported support from both the company and the union. Advisory board chair Bounlome Soumetho compared its teaching to Christian Sunday schools, focused on being moral, honest and respectful.
The same newspaper described the temple as still in operation in 2022. These attendance and staffing figures come from 2015 and may have changed.
keyFacts: 2004: Officially established near Worthington; the city's first Buddhist temple.
Nobles County changed its ordinances to allow a church in an agricultural area.
2015: Two resident monks; about 150 people at monthly services.
2015: Members came from southwestern Minnesota, South Dakota and Iowa.
institutions.connectToWork: If your outreach plan centers on the Twin Cities, how would you find out who it misses in greater Minnesota, and how far people travel to get what they need?

institutions.name: Wat Lao Buddhavas
body: In 1983, soon after the first Lao refugees arrived in Des Moines, the community bought a piece of land. The temple building was completed in 1997 and the rest of the grounds in 1999. Drake University's Comparison Project calls it the first Lao Buddhist temple in the city. Its two pages on the Des Moines temples spell the name Wat Lao Buddhavas and Wat Lao Buddhavath, and one explains that Wat Lao simply means Lao temple.

Drake describes a central temple with an altar, a residence for the monks, and two guest houses for visitors. Sunday services include chanting in Pali and a dharma talk in Lao, followed by a potluck. A Tak Bat, an offering of food to monks, is held about once a month, and an Ancestor's Day honors those who have died. Drake's guidance for visitors is to dress modestly, remove shoes, and not stretch your legs toward the altar or the monks.
By 2009 a second Lao temple in Des Moines, Wat Phothisomphan, had been established as a meditation monastery.
keyFacts: 1983: Land purchased by the Des Moines Lao community.
1997: Temple building completed.
1999: Grounds completed.
2009: Second Des Moines Lao temple, Wat Phothisomphan, established.
institutions.connectToWork: If you are invited to a gathering at a place of worship, how would you find out its expectations from the host beforehand, and who decides whether your visit is welcome?

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Lao means ethnic Lao people, who are distinct from Hmong, Khmu, Iu Mien and other peoples from Laos, so do not apply Hmong research here. No peer-reviewed study of how ethnic Lao families in the United States or Minnesota understand disability was found. What follows comes from one small study in Laos, a fact sheet that combines several Southeast Asian American groups, and one writer's own account.
questions: Who in your family should be part of this conversation or decision, if anyone?
What words do you and your family use for this? What would you like us to call it?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you, and is there anything you want it to avoid?
What do you think is going on, and what do you hope will help?
Does your temple, or any religious or traditional practice, matter for your care or your family's?
If you want to tell me, has anything in your history, including war or leaving your country, affected your health or the support you want?
Have past experiences with government offices or programs made you worried about using services? What would make this feel safer?
Which language do you want to use, in speech, sign and in writing, and do you read Lao script?
If someone in your family gives care: how is your own health, how alone do you feel in this, and would a break help?

context.heading: One small study from Laos
body: Low and colleagues surveyed 92 primary-school teachers in Luang Prabang, Laos, for a 2019 conference paper; 90 completed the survey. Reading descriptions of three children, many teachers saw autism characteristics as variations of typical young children's behavior and explained them as results of upbringing. The authors offer this as one way autism-related stigma may form in Laos. It is a preliminary study of teachers, not families, and not of Lao Americans.

The same paper says that scarce services in Laos meant only affluent families could afford a diagnosis and support, often by traveling to Thailand or Vietnam. People who came to the United States may therefore have had little contact with formal disability systems before arriving, but that is an inference, not a documented finding. Ask about each person's own history.

sources.label: Low and colleagues, International Conference on Special Education (2019)

context.heading: Faith and explanations
body: Writing about Buddhist communities in general often discusses karma as one explanation that some families give for disability. No source was found documenting this for Lao families, so do not assume it. If it comes up, let the person explain what it means to them. Spiritual and medical explanations can sit side by side.

Nor was any research found on how Lao families in the United States combine temple-based or traditional practices with disability services. Ask whether practices such as blessings, merit-making or monk visits matter, and make room for them in a plan when the person wants that.

sources.label: Low and colleagues, International Conference on Special Education (2019)

context.heading: Family caregiving
body: A Diverse Elders Coalition fact sheet, updated January 2023, reports its own survey of Southeast Asian American family caregivers. It lists Lao among many groups and gives figures for the whole group, not for Lao caregivers, and it does not state its sample size. It reports that 51 percent said they were the only person available to give care, 36 percent had difficulty with tasks such as translating health information, one quarter said caregiving harmed their physical or emotional health, and 22.7 percent felt isolated.

Lao American writer Lasamee Kettavong, in Mochi Magazine in 2025, describes care moving in every direction between grandparents, parents and children, often falling hardest on women. She writes that placing her father, a veteran of the Secret War in Laos who lived with PTSD, in a skilled nursing facility went against common norms but felt necessary. Neither facility had staff who spoke Lao, and family members acted as translators. He died during the pandemic. This is one person's experience, not a pattern.

sources.label: Diverse Elders Coalition, What Providers Should Know About Southeast Asian American Family Caregivers (updated January 2023)
Lasamee Kettavong, Mochi Magazine (May 23, 2025)

context.heading: Language, trust and system barriers
body: The same fact sheet reports limited English proficiency of 40 to 50 percent across Southeast Asian American communities, rising as high as 90 percent for elders. These are group figures with no Lao-only rate and no year stated. It reports a Laotian American poverty rate of 12.2 percent against a national 11.3 percent, also with no year. It links war and resettlement trauma, poor access to mental health services, and deportations to distrust of formal services. It recommends trained medical interpreters, translated materials, in-language caregiver support groups, funded partnerships with community organizations, and separate data for each group.

Use a trained Lao interpreter and confirm the person wants Lao and not Thai, Hmong or another language. Do not ask children to interpret. Before reading a missed appointment as cultural, check interpreter access, transport, hours and the agency's own rules.

sources.label: Diverse Elders Coalition, What Providers Should Know About Southeast Asian American Family Caregivers (updated January 2023)

context.heading: Words
body: No reliable source was found for Lao-language disability terms or for which terms carry stigma, so none are offered here. Low and colleagues report no official Lao term for autism at the time of their study. Do not use terms from memory or machine translation. Ask a qualified interpreter or the person which words they prefer. In English, follow the person's own preference. Deaf Lao Americans may use ASL, Lao Sign Language or home signs, so ask.

sources.label: Low and colleagues, International Conference on Special Education (2019)

context.heading: Disabled leadership and who is missing
body: Justin Phongsavanh, profiled on this page, is a Paralympic medalist and world record holder. No Lao American disability advocate or Minnesota organization led by disabled Lao people was found, though the search was limited. Do not take this as meaning none exist.

In Laos, the Lao Disabled People's Association has described itself as the country's main advocacy body for people with disabilities, working on rights training, employment, law reform and inclusion (2016 account). In February 2026 UNICEF Laos described young people with disabilities there training others on their rights, with sign language teachers among the facilitators. The youth advocate Khamta Sengmany said that many young people do not know what they are entitled to. These accounts show disabled people in Laos leading this work, and they describe no one here.

sources.label: University of Oregon IE Collaborative Laos, Lao Disabled People's Association (Feb. 11, 2016)
UNICEF Laos, We Are Not Alone (Feb. 25, 2026)

communityRoutes.name: Lao Assistance Center of Minnesota
communityRoutes.purpose: Lao-focused help with food, systems navigation, housing, employment, education and public benefits in Minneapolis. It does not list disability-specific services, so ask what it can do. Phone (612) 374-4967.

communityRoutes.name: Center for Lao Studies translation services
communityRoutes.purpose: Paid Lao-English document translation, with a second translator who edits and proofreads each document, in pre- or post-1975 Lao spelling. Ask which spelling your readers expect.

organizations.intro: Chanida Phaengdara Potter told MPR News in 2013 that Minnesota had the third-largest Lao population in the United States. In 2022 the American Immigration Council put the number of Lao people rebuilding their lives in the state at more than 13,000; it gives no source year or count method. People have organized through refugee-era agencies, Buddhist temples, the arts and shared events such as Lao New Year, which MPR reported bringing together more than 20 organizations in Crystal in 2013. No Minnesota Lao-language newspaper or broadcast outlet could be confirmed. These are starting points for learning. The list is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.name: The SEAD Project
entries.purpose: Founded in 2011, it works with Hmong, Khmer, Lao and Vietnamese communities through arts and storytelling, heritage and language programs, and leadership development. Its 2026 work includes the Colors of Southeast Asia festival and a digital archive, Mekong Journeys.

entries.name: Wat Lao Minnesota
entries.purpose: A Lao Buddhist temple in the south metro, with an IRS ruling year of 2005. No website or published program list was found, and the nonprofit record does not show current activity, so check before planning a visit.

entries.name: Lao Temple Vipassana Center of Minnesota
entries.purpose: A Lao Buddhist temple and meditation center, with an IRS ruling year of 2012. No working website or published program list was found, and the nonprofit record does not show current activity, so check before planning a visit.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: A nonprofit newsroom reporting for Minnesota's immigrants and communities of color, in English, founded in 2019. Lao items are occasional.

entries.name: MPR News
entries.purpose: Minnesota public radio news, in English. It has reported on Lao New Year, the Lao Assistance Center and Lao writers.

entries.name: SEARAC
entries.purpose: Founded in 1979, it works with Cambodian, Lao and Vietnamese American communities on separate data for each group, deportation, wellness and census policy, with active campaigns in October 2026.

entries.name: Sahtu Press
entries.purpose: A Lao American-owned publisher founded in 2013, with picture books, poetry and comics rooted in Lao history and family life. Its online articles cover Lao diaspora arts, including Minnesota events; its latest is dated October 19, 2026.

entries.name: Center for Lao Studies
entries.purpose: Research, education and information on Laos and its peoples, with Lao-English translation. It lists an international conference on Lao studies in Heidelberg for September 2026 and a study-abroad program for 2027.

entries.name: RFA Lao
entries.purpose: Lao-language news on Laos. Radio Free Asia announced in May 2025 that it was stopping new content in Lao, and as of October 2026 its Lao page again shows items dated that month.

entries.name: Laopost
entries.purpose: A Lao-language news site covering Laos, including government affairs, with items dated late October 2026. It is an outlet in Laos, not a U.S. diaspora paper.

entries.name: Lao News Agency
entries.purpose: The official state news agency of Laos, in Lao, English and French. Read it knowing that it is state-run.

entries.name: Vientiane Times
entries.purpose: An English-language paper established in 1994 as a department of a Lao ministry. The state news agency says it works under the supervision of Party and state leaders, so read it with that in mind.
